input:
Basis

This report presents the design of an amine absorber intended for a gas treatment duty. The design throughput of the unit is 43 t per day, and the removal duty is 88% of the key component present in the feed gas. The wetted parts of the equipment are constructed in 316L stainless steel. In essence, the absorber removes the key component from the gas by bringing it into contact with a circulating amine solvent: the gas enters at the base of the column and rises upwards through the internals while the solvent flows downwards, so that the key component is progressively transferred from the gas into the solvent. The rich solvent then leaves from the base of the column and passes to regeneration, while the treated gas leaves from the top. The design basis consists of the stated throughput together with the stated removal duty, and the sizing, materials and risks sections that follow are all developed from these two figures. It should be noted that feed conditions falling outside the stated basis, including any change in the content of the key component in the gas, would require the design to be returned to this section so that the basis could be restated. The solvent is regenerated outside the column and returned to service as lean solvent, and the scope of the absorber design is limited to the column itself together with its immediate auxiliaries.

Sizing

The column is sized on the basis of two requirements that are, to some extent, in conflict with one another. The diameter is governed by the hydraulic capacity of the internals, since the gas and liquid rates determine the flooding limit, and the diameter is selected in such a way that the design rates remain below this limit with the margin that is customarily held in standard practice for absorber service. The height, on the other hand, is governed by the separation that is to be achieved: the number of transfer units that is required in order to reach the stated removal duty, combined with the height of a transfer unit delivered by the chosen internals in amine service, gives the packed or trayed height of the column. The lean solvent circulation rate is the operating variable that links the two requirements together, because a higher rate of circulation increases the removal achieved at a given height while at the same time increasing the hydraulic load at a given diameter. The sizing therefore proceeds by first fixing the circulation rate from the removal duty, then checking the diameter against flooding at that rate, and finally setting the height from the transfer requirement. The auxiliaries are sized from the same rates, with the rich and lean solvent pumps being based on the circulation, the overhead system on the treated gas rate, and the regeneration feed on the rich solvent rate. No part of the sizing is based on a rate lying outside the stated basis, and any change in the basis would reopen both the diameter and the height, since the two are coupled through the circulation rate.

Materials

The wetted parts are specified in the stainless steel grade that is named in the basis. This selection is based on the corrosion behaviour that is characteristic of amine service. The solvent is corrosive in the regions where it is hot and loaded with the key component, and carbon steel in rich amine service is known to be subject both to general corrosion and to cracking at welds where residual stress is present. The grade that has been selected resists the general corrosion of the service and represents the established choice for wetted amine duty, and it is for this reason that the wetted parts do not require a corrosion allowance of the kind that would be needed in a carbon steel design. Parts that are not wetted by the solvent follow ordinary practice for gas service and are not specified in this report. It should be emphasised that the selection is made for the design solvent at its design strength, so that a change of solvent, or of solvent strength, would reopen the selection, and this question is accordingly dealt with in the risks section rather than here.

Risks

There are two items that remain open at the close of this report, and neither of them is resolved within it. The first of these is the fouling of the internals by solids or degradation products that are carried in the solvent, which has the effect of reducing the transfer area and increasing the pressure drop over the course of a run. No allowance has been made in the design for the rate of fouling, because no rate has been established for this duty, and the operating consequence, in the form of a shorter run between cleanings, is accepted as an open item rather than being designed out. The second item is turndown. At rates below the design throughput, the liquid distribution over the internals deteriorates and the removal falls accordingly, and the lowest rate at which the stated removal can still be achieved has not been established in this report. Both of these items bear on the operation of the unit rather than on its mechanical design, and both are carried forward to the operating review as stated limits on the design in the form in which it is issued.
target:
Basis

The report covers the design of an amine absorber for a gas treatment duty. The design throughput is 43 t per day, and the removal duty is 88% of the key component in the feed gas. Wetted parts are 316L stainless steel. The absorber removes the key component from the gas by contact with a circulating amine solvent: the gas enters at the base of the column and rises through the internals while the solvent flows down, and the key component passes from the gas into the solvent. The rich solvent leaves the base for regeneration, and the treated gas leaves at the top. The design basis is the stated throughput and the stated removal duty, and the sizing, materials and risks sections work from those two figures and from no others. Feed conditions outside the stated basis, including a change in the key component content of the gas, return the design to this section for restatement. The solvent is regenerated outside the column and returned as lean solvent, and the absorber design covers the column and its immediate auxiliaries only.

The regeneration of the solvent stands outside the column design, but its duty is fixed by the absorber: the rich solvent leaves at the loading the column delivers, and the lean solvent returns at the loading the removal duty assumes, so the two loadings are part of this basis and a change in either returns here.

Sizing

The column is sized on two requirements that pull against each other. The diameter is set by the hydraulic capacity of the internals: the gas and liquid rates fix the flooding limit, and the diameter is chosen so that the design rates stand below that limit with the margin that standard practice holds for absorber service. The height is set by the separation: the number of transfer units needed to reach the stated removal duty, at the height of a transfer unit that the chosen internals deliver in amine service, gives the packed or trayed height. The lean solvent circulation rate is the operating variable that connects the two requirements: a higher circulation raises the removal at a given height and raises the hydraulic load at a given diameter. Sizing therefore proceeds by fixing the circulation rate from the removal duty, checking the diameter against flooding at that rate, and setting the height from the transfer requirement, in that order. Auxiliaries are sized from the same rates: the rich and lean solvent pumps on the circulation, the overhead system on the treated gas rate, and the regeneration feed on the rich solvent rate. No part of the sizing rests on a rate outside the stated basis, and a change in the basis reopens the diameter and the height together, because the two are coupled through the circulation rate.

The internals themselves are part of the sizing result: distribution of the liquid over the top of the bed and collection and redistribution down its height are what make the transfer height assumed in the sizing available in the built column, and a distributor that wets the bed unevenly returns a removal below the design figure at the design rates.

Materials

The wetted parts are specified in the stainless steel grade named in the basis. The selection rests on the corrosion behaviour of amine service. The solvent is corrosive where it is hot and loaded with the key component, and carbon steel in rich amine service is subject to general corrosion and to cracking at welds where residual stress stands. The grade selected resists the general corrosion of the service and is the established choice for wetted amine duty. Its resistance is the reason the wetted parts carry no corrosion allowance of the kind a carbon steel design would need. Parts not wetted by the solvent follow ordinary practice for gas service and are not specified in this report. The selection is stated for the design solvent at its design strength: a change of solvent, or of solvent strength, reopens the selection, and that question stands in the risks section rather than here.

Corrosion monitoring of the wetted parts is by inspection at outages rather than by continuous measurement, and the selection carries that limitation with it: the grade is chosen for the design solvent, and the inspection interval is where a departure from the design solvent would first be seen.

Risks

Two items stand open at the close of the report, and neither is resolved in it. Fouling of the internals by solids or degradation products carried in the solvent reduces the transfer area and raises the pressure drop over a run. The design carries no allowance for the rate of fouling, because no rate is established for this duty, and the operating consequence, a shorter run between cleanings, is accepted as an open item rather than designed out. Turndown is the second item. At rates below the design throughput, the liquid distribution over the internals deteriorates and the removal falls with it, and the lowest rate at which the stated removal still holds is not established in the report. Both items bear on operation rather than on the mechanical design, and both are carried to the operating review as stated limits on the design as issued: the design stands on its stated basis, with fouling and turndown named as the limits of that basis. Monitoring of the two open items belongs to operation: fouling declares itself in the pressure drop trend, and turndown declares itself in the removal measured at low rate, and both trends are the records the operating review receives.
